title: Examination of the Four Noble Truths

slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-four: the examination of the four noble truths.

slides.heading: Does anything still matter?
points: If suffering is empty, why end it?
If the path is empty, why walk it?
If the Buddha is empty, who taught?
slides.say: Here is the worry that anyone meeting emptiness has sooner or later. If nothing has a nature of its own, does anything matter? If suffering is empty, why end it? If the path is empty, why walk it? If the Buddha is empty, who taught? It sounds as if emptiness, taken seriously, would dissolve the very teaching that teaches it, and leave us with nothing to stand on.

slides.heading: The turning point of the work
points: An opponent: you have destroyed Buddhism
Nagarjuna turns the charge around
Own-nature, not emptiness, would destroy the truths
slides.say: Chapter twenty-four meets this worry head on, and it is the turning point of the whole work. Up to here Nagarjuna has taken apart conditions, motion, self, time and much else. Now an opponent from his own tradition says: you have gone too far, you have destroyed Buddhism. Nagarjuna's answer turns the charge around completely. It is not emptiness that would destroy the four noble truths. It is the opposite of emptiness. Only because things are empty can anything arise, change, be practised or be attained.

slides.heading: The verses
points: Forty verses, a new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. There are forty of them. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: The objection: emptiness destroys everything
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter opens with the opponent's case, stated fairly and in full, in verses one to six. It runs like a row of dominoes. If everything is empty, nothing arises and nothing passes away. Then there are no four noble truths, because the truths are about the arising of suffering and its ending. Without the truths, there is nothing to understand, abandon, cultivate or realise: no practice. Without practice, no one reaches the stages of the noble path. Without those noble persons, there is no community; and without the truths, no teaching. Without teaching and community, how could there be a Buddha? So emptiness undermines all three jewels, and the fruits of action, right and wrong, and all the dealings of the world besides. The opponent is not a straw man. He is a serious Buddhist, probably of the Abhidharma schools, for whom the elements of experience had to have natures of their own in order to function. Everything hangs on the first box: he takes empty to mean non-existent.

slides.heading: You have misunderstood emptiness
points: Its purpose: to quiet elaborations
Itself: the absence of own-nature, not a void
Its meaning: dependent arising
slides.say: Nagarjuna does not deny that the chain would follow if emptiness meant what the opponent thinks. He says the opponent has misunderstood three things: the purpose of emptiness, emptiness itself, and the meaning of emptiness. Chandrakirti spells them out. The purpose of emptiness is to quiet elaborations, the mind's spinning-out of it is and it is not around things it takes to be there. Emptiness itself is not a thing, not a void and not a hidden absolute; it is the absence of own-nature. And the meaning of emptiness is dependent arising. The opponent has heard empty and pictured nothing at all. That picture is what troubles him, not emptiness.

slides.heading: The two truths
slides.say: To explain, Nagarjuna introduces the two truths. The Buddhas teach by relying on two: the conventional truth of the world, and the truth in the ultimate sense. Conventional truth is the world as it appears and works: tables hold cups, medicine heals, people suffer and are kind. Chandrakirti notes three senses of the word for conventional: what conceals, what exists in mutual dependence, and worldly convention, the naming and agreement we live by. Ultimate truth is what analysis finds when it looks for the table's own nature, apart from its parts, causes and name: no such nature is found. Not finding it is the ultimate truth, emptiness. The two truths are not two worlds, one false and one real, stacked on top of each other. They are one appearance, taken in two ways. A thing works because it depends, and because it depends it has no nature of its own.

slides.heading: Convention is the ladder
points: Without convention, the ultimate cannot be taught
Without the ultimate, nirvana is not reached
The ladder is not thrown away
slides.say: Whoever misses this distinction misses the depth of the Buddha's teaching. And the two truths need each other in a definite order. Without relying on convention, the ultimate cannot be taught: emptiness is pointed out using words, examples and reasoning, all of which belong to convention. And without coming to the ultimate, nirvana is not reached: liberation comes from seeing through the grasping at own-nature, not from rearranging conventions. Convention is the ladder; the ultimate is where it leads; and the ladder is not thrown away, because the ultimate is only ever the emptiness of conventional things.

slides.heading: A snake grasped the wrong way
slides.say: Emptiness is powerful, and like anything powerful it can harm. Wrongly seen, it ruins the one who sees it, like a snake picked up by the wrong end, or a spell said wrongly. Picked up behind the head, a snake is safe; picked up by the tail, it turns and bites. Emptiness has two wrong ends. Grasped as nothingness, it becomes nihilism: nothing matters, nothing has consequences. Grasped as a thing, an ultimate essence or cosmic ground, it becomes a new substance, the very reification it was meant to cure. Grasped correctly, it is simply the absence of own-nature in things that keep working. This danger, the tradition says, is why the Buddha hesitated to teach after his awakening. The faults the opponent charges against emptiness are real faults, but they belong to the nothingness he has mistaken it for.

slides.heading: Everything is possible
points: For whom emptiness is possible, everything is possible
To work is to depend
A thing with its own nature could neither act nor be acted on
slides.say: Then comes the verse at the centre of the chapter, and perhaps of the whole book, verse twenty-four point fourteen: for whom emptiness is possible, everything is possible; for whom emptiness is not possible, nothing is possible. The verb means is possible, fits, makes sense, and so works. Why? Because to work is to depend. A seed works by turning into a sprout, which means it is not fixed as a seed. Medicine works by changing a body, which means the illness was not fixed as illness. Practice works by changing a mind. Everything that functions does so by being open to conditions, and being open to conditions is exactly what empty of own-nature means. The opponent, Nagarjuna says, is like a man riding a horse who accuses others of stealing it. He relies on dependent arising every moment, and then charges the teaching of dependent arising with destroying cause and effect.

slides.heading: Dependent arising is emptiness
slides.say: If you see things as existing by their own nature, you see them as needing no causes or conditions, for what is complete in itself needs nothing else. Then you undermine everything causal. Verse twenty-four point eighteen gives Nagarjuna's positive statement, as close as he comes to one: dependent arising is what we call emptiness; that is a designation in dependence; and that itself is the middle way. Four names for one fact. Dependent arising is how things exist: only in dependence. Emptiness is what that means: no own-nature. Designation in dependence says that even emptiness is a name given in relation to what it qualifies, not a thing in its own right; Chandrakirti's commentary adds that dependent arising itself is designation in dependence, as a chariot is designated on its parts. And the middle way is the result: free of the extreme of existence by own-nature and of the extreme of nothingness. Verse nineteen concludes: there is nothing that has not arisen in dependence, so there is nothing that is not empty.

slides.heading: The objection turned around
slides.say: Now Nagarjuna repeats the opponent's first verse word for word, with one change: empty becomes not empty. If all this were not empty, there would be no arising and no passing away, and no four noble truths. Then he runs the whole chain again and shows that own-nature, not emptiness, breaks every link. Suffering with its own nature could not come and go; it would simply be, always. For the same reason it could never end. A path with its own nature could not be cultivated, because to cultivate is to bring about what was not there. What is by nature not yet understood could never come to be understood. One who is by nature not a Buddha would never become one, however hard he practised. No one could act rightly or wrongly, for what is not empty cannot be done or made. And the world would be unborn, unceasing and fixed like an anvil. So the chapter ends where it began, with the four truths, now secured: whoever sees dependent arising sees suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path.

slides.heading: Why own-nature freezes the world
slides.say: The reversal can seem like a clever trick, so it is worth seeing why it works. Picture a thing with a nature truly its own. Nothing else can change it, because if something could, its nature would depend on that thing not happening. And it cannot change itself, because a change would make it other than its own nature. So it is stuck. It cannot come into being from causes, and it cannot pass away. That is the sealed seed on one side of the diagram. The seed that can sprout is the empty seed. Emptiness is not a loss of the world. The world we actually live in, where seeds sprout, wounds heal, minds learn and suffering can end, is only possible as an empty world. A substance would not be a firmer foundation. It would be a stopped clock.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: The four truths, the path, the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha
Right and wrong, cause and effect
Conventional truth: the truth we live and practise by
slides.say: Everything the opponent feared to lose is kept, and kept on firmer ground: the four noble truths, the path and its fruits, the Buddha, the teaching and the community, right and wrong, cause and effect, and the whole web of ordinary dealings. Conventional truth is not demoted. It is the truth by which we live, act and practise, and the only way the ultimate can be taught at all. What goes is only own-nature, the idea that things are what they are from their own side, sealed off from conditions.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: A habit you have changed
A skill you have learned, a grief that has softened
Each was possible because the old state was not fixed
slides.say: You can test the verse at any moment. Think of a habit you have changed, a skill you have learned, a grief that has softened. Each change was possible only because the old state was not fixed. That openness is emptiness, at work in your own life.

slides.heading: In the books
points: The chapter the two books cite most often
Substrateless World: Interlude and Chapters 2–6, 11, 14, 15
The Logic of Dependency; A Beginner's Companion
slides.say: This is the chapter the two books cite most often. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: the Introduction, on emptiness seized by the wrong end; the Interlude, on dependent arising as a dependent designation and the ultimate taught only through convention; chapter two, on why nothing escapes dependence; chapter three, on the charge of nihilism and the horse; chapters four and five, on relation, interaction and the two truths; chapter six, on emptiness and nothingness; chapters eleven and fourteen, on agency and function; chapter fifteen, on why it is not emptiness that would freeze the world; and the Conclusion, on freedom. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, and A Beginner's Companion in The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness take it up too, and two talks on YouTube, Core Logic Five and Mipham's two models of the two truths. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter twenty-five, the examination of nirvana.
